query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating forms a self-healing, ultrafine protective oxide scale—primarily a mixed oxide incorporating copper along with Fe, Ni, Co, and Cr—that dynamically refines the near-surface microstructure, reduces the coefficient of friction, and suppresses wear by acting as a load–bearing and lubricious barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating on a conventional metal substrate, exhibiting a uniform, nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure without a pre-formed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Expose the coating to a controlled high-temperature regime (e.g., 650–900 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere prior to and during wear testing, as opposed to the baseline room-temperature coating condition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests under cyclic loading in air, with temperatures maintained between approximately 650 °C and 900 °C; loads representative of service conditions in high-temperature applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A dynamically formed, ultrafine (nano-scaled) protective oxide layer (including copper oxides and mixed oxides of Fe, Ni, Co, and Cr) that evolves during high-temperature exposure and wear.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated oxidation at high temperatures induces rapid formation of a thin, coherent oxide scale that repairs itself under wear conditions. This ultrananocrystalline layer reduces friction and minimizes direct substrate contact, thereby decreasing adhesive and abrasive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, high-temperature wear tests should reveal a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates compared to room-temperature conditions. Post-test microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) and surface analysis (e.g., XPS) would show a continuous, ultrafine mixed oxide layer at the coating surface, with signs of dynamic regeneration during wear.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coatings tested at room temperature without pre-oxidation, which do not develop the protective oxide layer and exhibit higher wear rates and friction.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected to occur within the 650–900 °C temperature range under typical cyclic sliding loads; outside these boundaries (e.g., much lower temperatures with insufficient oxidation or excessively high temperatures causing oxide spallation), the mechanism and wear resistance may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition, phase distribution, and durability of the protective oxide scale under prolonged wear and variable thermal cycling remain uncertain. In addition, the individual contributions of copper oxidation versus the oxidation of other constituent elements require further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on identical metal substrates. One set is subjected to a high-temperature pre-treatment (650–900 °C in air) to induce oxide scale formation, while the other is kept at room temperature. Both sets are then tested under identical cyclic sliding wear conditions in an oxidizing environment. Detailed surface characterization (SEM, TEM, XPS) is performed before and after wear testing.
measurements: Wear rate and volume loss using profilometry or weight loss measurements
Coefficient of friction during wear tests
Chemical composition and phase identification of surface oxides using XPS or XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-temperature pre-treated coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and friction compared to the room-temperature baseline, or if post-test analysis fails to reveal the formation of a coherent, ultrafine protective oxide layer, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Combining Machine Learning and Molecular Dynamics to Predict Mechanical Properties and Microstructural Evolution of FeNiCrCoCu High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractCompared with traditional alloys, high-entropy alloys have better mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. However, their mechanical properties and microstructural evolution behavior are unclear due to their complex composition. Machine learning has powerful data processing and analysis capabilities, that provides technical advantages for in-depth study of the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys. Thus, we combined machine learning and molecular dynamics to predict the mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloys. The optimal multiple linear regression machine learning algorithm predicts that the optimal composition is Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy, with a tensile strength of 28.25 GPa. Furthermore, molecular dynamics is used to verify the predicted mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys, and it is found that the error between the tensile strength predicted by machine learning and the tensile strength obtained by molecular dynamics simulation is within 0.5%. Microstructure, Mechanical and Tribological Properties of High-Entropy Carbide (MoNbTaTiV)C5

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy carbide (NbTaTiV)C4 (HEC4), (MoNbTaTiV)C5 (HEC5), and (MoNbTaTiV)C5-SiC (HEC5S) multiphase ceramics were prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1900 to 2100 °C, using metal carbide and silicon carbide (SiC) as raw materials. Their microstructure, and mechanical and tribological properties were investigated. The results showed that the (MoNbTaTiV)C5 synthesized at 1900–2100 °C had a face-centered cubic structure and density higher than 95.6%. The increase in sintering temperature was conducive to the promotion of densification, growth of grains, and diffusion of metal elements. The introduction of SiC helped to promote densification but weakened the strength of the grain boundaries. The average specific wear rates for HEC4 were within an order of magnitude of 10−5 mm3/N·m, and for HEC5 and HEC5S were within a range of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/N·m. The wear mechanism of HEC4 was abrasion, while that of HEC5 and HEC5S was mainly oxidation wear.Keywords: high-entropy carbides, multiphase ceramics, friction and wear properties

Microstructure and Corrosive Wear Properties of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy Coatings

Abstract: AbstractIn order to improve the wear resistance of offshore drilling equipment, CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared by cold spraying (CS) and high-speed oxygen fuel spraying (HVOF), and the coatings were subjected to vacuum heat treatment at different temperatures (500 °C, 700 °C and 900 °C). The friction and wear experiments of the coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment were carried out in simulated seawater drilling fluid. The results show that CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings prepared by CS and HVOF have dense structure and bond well with the substrate. After vacuum heat treatment, the main peaks of all oriented FCC phases are broadened and the peak strength is obviously enhanced. The two types of coatings achieve maximum hardness after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C; the Vickers microhardness of CS-500 °C and HVOF-500 °C are 487.6 and 352.4 HV0.1, respectively.
